But Eli's sons, unsatisfied with the breast and shoulder, which were the perquisites appointed to them by the divine law (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.27">Ex 29:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.31">Le 7:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.32">32</reference>), not only claimed part of the offerer's share, but rapaciously seized them previous to the sacred ceremony of heaving or waving (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.29">Le 7:29</reference>); and moreover they committed the additional injustice of taking up with their fork those portions which they preferred, while still raw. Pious people revolted at such rapacious and profane encroachments on the dues of the altar, as well as what should have gone to constitute the family and social feast of the offerer. The truth is, the priests having become haughty and unwilling in many instances to accept invitations to those feasts, presents of meat were sent to them; and this, though done in courtesy at first, being, in course of time, established into a right, gave rise to all the rapacious keenness of Eli's sons.<div eID="gen3393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3394" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.18-1Sam.2.26">1Sa 2:18-26</reference>. Samuel's Ministry. <div eID="gen3394" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d07381bda8ff097cea0aeb729c73794c0adce78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2518"/><div sID="gen3395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2518"/><hi type="bold">18. But Samuel ministered before the Lord, being a child--</hi>This notice of his early services in the outer courts of the tabernacle was made to pave the way for the remarkable prophecy regarding the high priest's family.<div eID="gen3395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">girded with a linen ephod--</hi>A small shoulder-garment or apron, used in the sacred service by the inferior priests and Levites; sometimes also by judges or eminent persons, and hence allowed to Samuel, who, though not a Levite, was devoted to God from his birth. <div eID="gen3396" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fc684df4b714a9f193940f05ccdd3628a3f597f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2519"/><div sID="gen3397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2519"/><hi type="bold">19. his mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year--</hi>Aware that he could not yet render any useful service to the tabernacle, she undertook the expense of supplying him with wearing apparel. All weaving stuffs, manufacture of cloth, and making of suits were anciently the employment of women. <div eID="gen3397" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bbeb1c05c92b6e86e597480168dcde5f32bfc6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2520"/><div sID="gen3398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2520"/><hi type="bold">20. Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife--</hi>This blessing, like that which he had formerly pronounced, had a prophetic virtue; which, before long, appeared in the increase of Hannah's family (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.21">1Sa 2:21</reference>), and the growing qualifications of Samuel for the service of the sanctuary. <div eID="gen3398" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7aa992b28044ea001bc3848e2d7b9acc27c02b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2521"/><div sID="gen3399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2521"/><hi type="bold">22-24. the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle--</hi>This was an institution of holy women of a strictly ascetic order, who had relinquished worldly cares and devoted themselves to the Lord; an institution which continued down to the time of Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Lu 2:37</reference>). Eli was, on the whole, a good man, but lacking in the moral and religious training of his family. He erred on the side of parental indulgence; and though he reprimanded them (see on <reference osisRef="Deut.21.18">De 21:18</reference>), yet, from fear or indolence, he shrank from laying on them the restraints, or subjecting them to the discipline, their gross delinquencies called for. In his judicial capacity, he winked at their flagrant acts of maladministration and suffered them to make reckless encroachments on the constitution, by which the most serious injuries were inflicted both on the rights of the people and the laws of God. <div eID="gen3399" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f5c65cdb60b79c34f4c92c733119c8524b6084e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2522"/><div sID="gen3400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2522"/><hi type="bold">25. they hearkened not unto the voice of their father, because--</hi>it should be therefore.<div eID="gen3400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord would slay them--</hi>It was not God's preordination, but their own wilful and impenitent disobedience which was the cause of their destruction.<div eID="gen3401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3402" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27-1Sam.2.35">1Sa 2:27-35</reference>. A Prophecy against Eli's House. <div eID="gen3402" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0c100b27ba531e3619b658ff03b05b51ea7e3a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2523"/><div sID="gen3403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2523"/><hi type="bold">27. there came a man of God unto Eli, and said ... that there shall not be an old man in thine house--</hi>So much importance has always, in the East, been attached to old age, that it would be felt to be a great calamity, and sensibly to lower the respectability of any family which could boast of few or no old men. The prediction of this prophet was fully confirmed by the afflictions, degradation, poverty, and many untimely deaths with which the house of Eli was visited after its announcement (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.11">1Sa 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.18-1Sam.22.23">22:18-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.27">1Ki 2:27</reference>). <div eID="gen3403" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b5dc069e598d75b4af634e838faaebe865384e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2524"/><div sID="gen3404" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2524"/><hi type="bold">31. I will cut off thine arm, and the arm of thy father's house--</hi>By the withdrawal of the high priesthood from Eleazar, the elder of Aaron's two sons (after Nadab and Abihu were destroyed, [Nu 3:4]), that dignity had been conferred on the family of Ithamar, to which Eli belonged, and now that his descendants had forfeited the honor, it was to be taken from them and restored to the elder branch. <div eID="gen3404" type="x-p"/>
entries.29c3e088ec536e3af22e77aea87ca7c211ca8178: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2525"/><div sID="gen3405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2525"/><hi type="bold">32. thou shalt see an enemy in my habitation--</hi>A successful rival for the office of high priest shall rise out of another family (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.35">2Sa 15:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.22">29:22</reference>). But the marginal reading, "thou shalt see the affliction of the tabernacle," seems to be a preferable translation. <chapter eID="1Sam.2"/>

entries.ab83b52b95f0c56cb4477bb25fe30b434670ace9: <div eID="gen9484" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9487" type="x-p"/> Hannah's prophetic hymn, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1-1Sam.2.10">1Sam 2:1-10</reference>. Samuel ministers to the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.11">1Sam 2:11</reference>. The abominable conduct of Eli's sons, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.12-1Sam.2.17">1Sam 2:12-17</reference>. Farther account of Samuel, and of the Divine blessing on Elkanah and Hannah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.18-1Sam.2.21">1Sam 2:18-21</reference>. Eli's reprehensible remissness towards his sons in not restraining them in their great profligacy, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.22-1Sam.2.26">1Sam 2:22-26</reference>. The message of God to Eli, and the prophecy of the downfall of his family, and slaughter of his wicked sons Hophni and Phinehas, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27-1Sam.2.36">1Sam 2:27-36</reference>. <div eID="gen9487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9488" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9489" type="x-p"/> And Hannah prayed, and said - The Chaldee very properly says, And Hannah prayed in the spirit of prophecy; for indeed the whole of this prayer, or as it may be properly called oracular declaration, is a piece of regular prophecy, every part of it having respect to the future, and perhaps not a little - of it declaratory oil the Messiah's kingdom. <div eID="gen9489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9490" type="x-p"/> Dr. Hales has some very good observations on this prophetic song. "This admirable hymn excels in simplicity of composition, closeness of connection, and uniformity of sentiment; breathing the pious effusions of a devout mind, deeply impressed with a conviction of God's mercies to herself in particular, and of his providential government of the world in general; exalting the poor in spirit or the humble-minded, and abasing the rich and the arrogant; rewarding the righteous, and punishing the wicked. Hannah was also a prophetess of the first class, besides predicting her own fruitfulness, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1Sam 2:5</reference>, (for she bore six children in all, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.21">1Sam 2:21</reference>), she foretold not only the more immediate judgments of God upon the Philistines during her son's administration, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.10">1Sam 2:10</reference>, but his remoter judgments 'upon the ends of the earth,' <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.10">1Sam 2:10</reference>, in the true spirit of the prophecies of Jacob, Balaam, and Moses. Like them, she describes the promised Savior of the world as a King, before there was any king in Israel; and she first applied to him the remarkable epithet Messiah in Hebrew, Christ in Greek, and Anointed in English, which was adopted by David, Nathan, Ethan, Isaiah, Daniel, and the succeeding prophets of the Old Testament; and by the apostles and inspired writers of the New. And the allusion thereto by Zacharias, the father of the Baptist, in his hymn, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.69">Luk 1:69</reference>, where he calls Christ a 'horn of salvation,' and the beautiful imitation of it by the blessed Virgin throughout in her hymn, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.46-Luk.1.55">Luk 1:46-55</reference>, furnishing the finest commentary thereon, clearly prove that Hannah in her rejoicing had respect to something higher than Peninnah her rival, or to the triumphs of Samuel, or even of David himself; the expressions are too magnificent and sublime to be confined to such objects. Indeed the learned rabbi, David Kimchi, was so struck with them that he ingenuously confessed that 'the King of whom Hannah speaks is the Messiah,' of whom she spake either by prophecy or tradition; for, continues he, 'there was a tradition among the Israelites, that a great zing should arise in Israel; and she seals up her song with celebrating this King who was to deliver them from all their enemies.' The tradition, as we have seen, was founded principally on Balaam's second and third prophecies, <reference osisRef="Num.24.7-Num.24.17">Num 24:7-17</reference>; and we cannot but admire that gracious dispensation of spiritual gifts to Hannah (whose name signifies grace) in ranking her among the prophets who should first unfold a leading title of the blessed Seed of the woman." <div eID="gen9490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9491" type="x-p"/> In the best MSS. the whole of this hymn is written in hemistich or poetic lines. I shall here produce it in this order, following the plan as exhibited in Kennicott's Bible, with some trifling alterations of our present version: - <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sam 2:1</reference>. My heart exulteth in Jehovah; My horn is exalted in Jehovah. My mouth is incited over mine enemies, For I have rejoiced in thy salvation. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.2">1Sam 2:2</reference>. There is none holy like Jehovah, For there is none besides thee; There is no rock like our God. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sam 2:3</reference>. Do not magnify yourselves, speak not proudly, proudly. Let not prevarication come out of your mouth; For the God of knowledge is Jehovah, And by him actions are directed. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4">1Sam 2:4</reference>. The bows of the heroes are broken, And the tottering are girded with strength. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1Sam 2:5</reference>. The full have hired out themselves for bread, And the famished cease for ever. The barren hath borne seven, And she who had many children is greatly enfeebled. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.6">1Sam 2:6</reference>. Jehovah killeth, and maketh alive; He bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.7">1Sam 2:7</reference>. Jehovah maketh poor, and maketh rich; He bringeth down, and he even exalteth. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sam 2:8</reference>. He lifteth up the poor from the dust; From the dunghill he exalteth the beggar, To make him sit with the nobles, And inherit the throne of glory. For to Jehovah belong the pillars of the earth, And upon them he hath placed the globe. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.9">1Sam 2:9</reference>. The foot of his saints he shall keep, And the wicked shall be silent in darkness; For by strength shall no man prevail. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.10">1Sam 2:10</reference>. Jehovah shall bruise them who contend with him; Upon them shall be thunder in the heavens. Jehovah shall judge the ends of the earth; And he shall give strength to his King. And shall exalt the horn of his Messiah. <div eID="gen9491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9492" type="x-p"/> It is not particularly stated here when Hannah composed or delivered this hymn; it appears from the connection to have been at the very time in which she dedicated her son to God at the tabernacle, though some think that she composed it immediately on the birth of Samuel. The former sentiment is probably the most correct. <div eID="gen9492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9493" type="x-p"/> Mine horn is exalted in the Lord - We have often seen that horn signifies power, might, and dominion. It is thus constantly used in the Bible, and was so used among the heathens. The following words of Horace to his jar are well known, and speak a sentiment very similar to that above: - <div eID="gen9493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9494" type="x-p"/> Tu spem reducis mentibus anxiis, <div eID="gen9494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> Viresque et addis Cornua pauperi. <div eID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> Hor. Odar. lib. iii., Od. 21, v. 18. <div eID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9497" type="x-p"/> Thou bringest back hope to desponding minds; And thou addest strength and horns to the poor man. <div eID="gen9497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9498" type="x-p"/> Paraphrastically expressed by Mr. Francis: - "Hope, by thee, fair fugitive, <div eID="gen9498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9499" type="x-p"/> Bids the wretched strive to live. <div eID="gen9499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9500" type="x-p"/> To the beggar you dispense <div eID="gen9500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9501" type="x-p"/> Heart and brow of confidence." <div eID="gen9501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9502" type="x-p"/> In which scarcely any thing of the meaning is preserved. <div eID="gen9502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9503" type="x-p"/> My mouth is enlarged - My faculty of speech is incited, stirred up, to express God's disapprobation against my adversaries.
entries.06cef33e73ccefb41846dee8828615f278a9d8f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9504" type="x-p"/> None holy - Holiness is peculiar to the God of Israel; no false god ever pretended to holiness; it was no attribute of heathenism, nor of any religion ever professed in the world before or since the true revelation of the true God. <div eID="gen9504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9505" type="x-p"/> There is none beside thee - There can be but one unoriginated, infinite, and eternal Being; that Being is Jehovah. <div eID="gen9505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9506" type="x-p"/> Any rock like our God - Rabbi Maimon has observed that the word צור tsur, which we translate rock, signifies, when applied to Jehovah, fountain, source, spring. There is no source whence continual help and salvation can arise but our God.
entries.6e637adb741f38c327eef951c9e925d99d4411fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9507" type="x-p"/> A God of knowledge - He is the most wise, teaching all good, and knowing all things. <div eID="gen9507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9508" type="x-p"/> Actions are weighed - נתכנו nithkenu, they are directed; it is by his counsel alone that we can successfully begin, continue, or end, any work.
entries.5d3ad00bd9c2dbc5f077e0a61a7fc4d201238d59: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9509" type="x-p"/> The bows of the mighty - The Targum considers the first verse as including a prophecy against the Philistines; the second verse, against Sennacherib and his army; the third, against Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans; the fourth, against the Greeks; the fifth, against Haman and his posterity; and the tenth, against Magog, and the enemies of the Messiah.
entries.08e4dd6e6d2af888c3ec2adfb31286d59b9028b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9510" type="x-p"/> They that were full - All the things mentioned in these verses frequently happen in the course of the Divine providence; and indeed it is the particular providence of God that Hannah seems more especially to celebrate through the whole of this simple yet sublime ode.
entries.5ae6fed27100fcf9ab03f27148a70ad01d9aeb7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen9510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9511" type="x-p"/> The Lord killeth - God is the arbiter of life and death; he only can give life, and he only has a right to take it away. <div eID="gen9511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9512" type="x-p"/> He bringeth down to the grave - The Hebrew word שאול sheol, which we translate grave, seems to have the same meaning in the Old Testament with ἁδης, hades in the New, which is the word generally used by the Septuagint for the other. It means the grave, the state of the dead, and the invisible place, or place of separate spirits. Sometimes we translate it hell, which now means the state of perdition, or place of eternal torments; but as this comes from the Saxon, to cover or conceal, it means only the covered place. In some parts of England the word helling is used for the covers of a book, the slating of a house, etc. The Targum seems to understand it of death and the resurrection. "He kills and commands to give life; he causes to descend into Sheol, that in the time to come he may bring them into the lives of eternity," i.e., the life of shame and everlasting contempt, and the life of glory.
entries.6abc3393b6b31981cb8f0dfac19da80cd0748f57: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9513" type="x-p"/> The Lord maketh poor - For many cannot bear affluence, and if God should continue to trust them with riches, they would be their ruin. <div eID="gen9513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9514" type="x-p"/> Maketh rich - Some he can trust, and therefore makes them stewards of his secular bounty.
entries.b2d7669b6fcc6af9c5a54c340c56dac681e06aab: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9515" type="x-p"/> To set them among princes - There have been many cases where, in the course of God's providence, a person has been raised from the lowest and most abject estate to the highest; from the plough to the imperial dignity: from the dungeon to the throne; from the dunghill to nobility. The story of Cincinnatus is well known; so is that of the patriarch Joseph; but there is one not less in point, that of Roushen Akhter, who was brought out of a dungeon, and exalted to the throne of Hindustan. On this circumstance the following elegant couplet was made: - "He was a bright star, but now is become a moon, <div eID="gen9515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> Joseph is taken from prison, and is become a king." <div eID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9517" type="x-p"/> There is a play here on Roushen Akhter, which signifies a bright star; and there is an allusion to the history of the patriarch Joseph, because of the similarity of fortune between him and the Mohammedan prince. <div eID="gen9517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9518" type="x-p"/> For the pillars of the earth are the Lord's - He is almighty, and upholds all things by the word of his power.
entries.44745ccc0b0b5d359fefc7d3f279d1f8c570582b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen9518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9519" type="x-p"/> He will keep the feet of his saints - He will order and direct all their goings, and keep them from every evil way. <div eID="gen9519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9520" type="x-p"/> The wicked shall be silent in darkness - The Targum understands this of their being sent to the darkness of hell; they shall be slain. <div eID="gen9520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9521" type="x-p"/> By strength shall no man prevail - Because God is omnipotent, and no power can be successfully exerted against him.
entries.564ee77e2a1234113679b8d0a2110b392ab2bc7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9522" type="x-p"/> The adversaries of the Lord shall be broken - Those who contend with him, מריביו meribaiu, by sinning against his laws, opposing the progress of his word, or persecuting his people. <div eID="gen9522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9523" type="x-p"/> Shall judge the ends on the earth - His empire shall be extended over all mankind by the preaching of the everlasting Gospel, for to this the afterpart of the verse seems to apply: He shall give strength unto his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ, or, as the Targum says, וירבי מלכות משיחיה viribbey malcuth Meshicheyh, "he shall multiply the kingdom of the Messiah." Here the horn means spiritual as well as secular dominion. <div eID="gen9523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9524" type="x-p"/> After the clause, The adversaries of the Lord shall be broken to pieces, the Septuagint add the following words: Μη καυχασθω ὁ φρονιμος εν τῃ φρονησει αυτου, κ. τ. λ. Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glorieth rather glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth the Lord; and that he executeth judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth. This is a very long addition, and appears to be taken from <reference osisRef="Jer.9.23">Jer 9:23</reference>, but on collating the two places the reader will find the words to be materially different. This clause is wanting in the Complutensian Polyglot, but it is in the edition of Aldus, in that of Cardinal Caroffa, and in the Codex Alexandrinus.
entries.ffb0383398c54860c5ecedc8e924d5dce367e8be: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen9524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9525" type="x-p"/> And Elkanah went to Ramah - Immediately after the 10th verse, the Septuagint add, Και κατελιπεν αυτον εκει ενωπιον Κυριου· και απηλθεν εις Αραματαια, And she left him there before the Lord, and went unto Arimathea. Thus the Septuagint suppose that the song of Hannah was composed when she brought Samuel to present him to the Lord; and as soon as she had completed this fine ode, she delivered him into the hands of Eli the high priest, and the child entered immediately on his ministration, under the direction and instructions of Eli.
entries.998d072eaec3ab35703f109d7fc16170b5fb35eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9526" type="x-p"/> The sons of Eli were sons of Belial - They were perverse, wicked, profligate men; devil's children. They knew not the Lord. "They know! nor would an angel show Him; They would not know, nor choose to know Him." <div eID="gen9526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9527" type="x-p"/> These men were the principal cause of all the ungodliness of Israel. Their most execrable conduct, described <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13-1Sam.2.17">1Sam 2:13-17</reference>, caused the people to abhor the Lord's offering. An impious priesthood is the grand cause of the transgressions and ruin of any nation; witness France, Germany, Spain, Ac., from 1792 to 1814.
entries.1d8f80edde0eea2ac9d278acf133e2e9e6879c8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9528" type="x-p"/> When any man offered sacrifice - That is, when a peace-offering was brought, the right shoulder and the breast belonged to the priest, the fat was burnt upon the altar, and the blood was poured at the bottom of the altar; the rest of the flesh belonged to the offerer. Under pretense of taking only their own part, they took the best of all they chose, and as much as they chose.
entries.60555fc6fc9e06353534569cd52034df40fff0fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen9528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9529" type="x-p"/> Kettle - caldron, or pot - We know not what these were, nor of what capacity; nor is it of any consequence.
entries.5674684ecfb9cb8c8c837c63391fa774cf68e242: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen9529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9530" type="x-p"/> Before they burnt the fat - They would serve themselves before God was served! This was iniquity and arrogance of the first magnitude. <div eID="gen9530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9531" type="x-p"/> He will not have sodden flesh - He chooses roast meat, not boiled; and if they had it in the pot before the servant came, he took it out that it might be roasted.
entries.2464fd1bbcd18d82db0fa5fb9a2dd47ba67fadce: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen9531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9532" type="x-p"/> Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great - That is, Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli. <div eID="gen9532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9533" type="x-p"/> Men abhorred the offering - As the people saw that the priests had no piety, and that they acted as if there was no God; they despised God's service, and became infidels. <div eID="gen9533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9534" type="x-p"/> A national priesthood, when the foundation is right, may be a great blessing; but if the priesthood becomes corrupt, though the foundation itself stand sure, the corruption of the national manners will be the unavoidable consequence.
entries.655cf420737d7fc2b94439112c45db7d3913d631: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen9534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9535" type="x-p"/> Girded with a linen ephod - This the Targum translates אסיר כרדוט דבוץ asir cardut debuts, "Girded with a cardit of byssus, or fine linen." The word cardut they seem to have borrowed from the Greek χειριδωτος, a tunic, having χειριδας, i.e., sleeves that came down to, or covered, the hands. This was esteemed an effeminate garment among the Romans. See Buxtorf's Talmudic Lexicon.
entries.63e3c44f4af9b8521214de15860b3c092bd71edc: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen9535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9536" type="x-p"/> Made him a little coat - מעיל קטן meil katon, a little cloak, or surtout, an upper garment: probably intended to keep him from the cold, and to save his other clothes from being abused in his meaner services. It is probable that she furnished him with a new one each year, when she came up to one of the annual sacrifices.
entries.5379883bc7b0ceca7112d34e8bd84ae45c7e6ac4: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen9536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9537" type="x-p"/> Eli blessed Elkanah - The natural place of this verse seems to be before the 11th; after which the 21st should come in; after the 21st, perhaps the 26th should come in. The subjects in this chapter seem very much entangled and confused by the wrong position of the verses.
entries.00661df6719bc47225b55b796ba526c9f478a506: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen9537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9538" type="x-p"/> They lay with the women that assembled - It is probable that these were persons who had some employment about the tabernacle. See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.38.8">Exo 38:8</reference>, where the Hebrew text is similar to that in this place.
entries.6a1b9a49a5c51cf4588b3ac2a750e3849651b19d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen9538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9539" type="x-p"/> Why do ye such things! - Eli appears to have been a fondly affectionate, easy father, who wished his sons to do well, but did not bring them under proper discipline, and did not use his authority to restrain them. As judge, he had power to cast them immediately out of the vineyard, as wicked and unprofitable servants; this he did not, and his and their ruin was the consequence.
entries.5b7cfa84379565ce8073f2a42a3f067c99bde124: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen9539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9540" type="x-p"/> If one man sin against another - All differences between man and man may be settled by the proper judge; but if a man sin against the Supreme Judge, God himself, who shall reconcile him to his Maker? Your sin is immediately against God himself, and is the highest insult that can be offered, because it is in the matter of his own worship, therefore ye may expect his heaviest judgments. <div eID="gen9540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9541" type="x-p"/> But if a man sin against the Lord, who shall entreat for him? - This was a question of the most solemn importance under the old covenant, especially after the death of Moses, the mediator. The law had determined what sins should be punished with death; and it was supposed that there was not any appeal from the decision there pronounced. <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.1">1Jn 2:1</reference> is an answer to this question; but it is an answer which the Gospel alone can give: My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not; but if any man sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. <div eID="gen9541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9542" type="x-p"/> Because the Lord would slay them - The particle כי ki, which we translate because, and thus make their continuance in sin the effect of God's determination to destroy them, should be translated therefore, as it means in many parts of the sacred writings. See Noldius's Particles, where the very text in question is introduced: Sed non auscultarunt, etc., Ideo voluit Jehova eos interficere; "But they would not hearken, etc.; Therefore God purposed to destroy them." It was their not hearkening that induced the Lord to will their destruction.
entries.eb716510858d16548879e87b849b4c4176c117a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen9542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9543" type="x-p"/> There came a man of God - Who this was we know not, but the Chaldee terms him נביא דיי nebiya daya, a prophet of Jehovah. <div eID="gen9543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9544" type="x-p"/> Unto the house of thy father - That is, to Aaron; he was the first high priest; the priesthood descended from him to his eldest son Eleazar, then to Phinehas. It became afterwards established in the younger branch of the family of Aaron; for Eli was a descendant of Ithamar, Aaron's youngest son. From Eli it was transferred back again to the family of Eleazar, because of the profligacy of Eli's sons.
entries.f164c7d2aeb244a49cea94d988db4a9c8a604c7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen9544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9545" type="x-p"/> And did I choose him - The high priesthood was a place of the greatest honor that could be conferred on man, and a place of considerable emolument; for from their part of the sacrifices they derived a most comfortable livelihood.
entries.8f4b077b66a73f14aa535b78524dff3a45fe751b: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen9545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9546" type="x-p"/> Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice - They disdained to take the part allowed by law; and would take for themselves what part they pleased, and as much as they pleased, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13-1Sam.2.16">1Sam 2:13-16</reference> : thus they kicked at the sacrifices. <div eID="gen9546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9547" type="x-p"/> Honourest thy sons above me - Permitting them to deal, as above, with the offerings and sacrifices, and take their part before the fat, etc., was burnt unto the Lord: thus they were first served. At this Eli connived, and thus honored his sons above God.
entries.65d1d05531830576201c026b80b7ac919b54fcd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen9547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9548" type="x-p"/> Should walk before me for ever - See <reference osisRef="Exo.29.9">Exo 29:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.40.15">Exo 40:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.25.10-Num.25.13">Num 25:10-13</reference>, where it is positively promised that the priesthood should be continued in the family of Aaron For Ever. But although this promise appears to be absolute, yet we plainly see that, like all other apparently absolute promises of God, it is conditional, i.e., a condition is implied though not expressed. <div eID="gen9548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9549" type="x-p"/> But now - be it far from me - You have walked unworthily; I shall annul my promise, and reverse my ordinance. See <reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">Jer 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.10">Jer 18:10</reference>. <div eID="gen9549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9550" type="x-p"/> For them that honor me - This is a plan from which God will never depart; this can have no alteration; every promise is made in reference to it; "they who honor God shall be honored; they who despise him shall be lightly esteemed."
entries.3bbdf03bd95cf27ebee9fb968a79d52b3928d334: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen9550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9551" type="x-p"/> I will cut off thine arm - I will destroy the strength, power, and influence of thy family.
entries.60ce32cd2733f5f8c2fd339b45912d0b1a562dfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen9551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9552" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt see an enemy in my habitation - Every version and almost every commentator understands this clause differently. The word צר tsar, which we translate an enemy, and the Vulgate aemulum, a rival, signifies calamity; and this is the best sense to understand it in here. The calamity which he saw was the defeat of the Israelites, the capture of the ark, the death of his wicked sons, and the triumph of the Philistines. All this he saw, that is, knew to have taken place, before he met with his own tragical death. <div eID="gen9552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9553" type="x-p"/> In all the wealth which God shall give Israel - This also is dark. The meaning may be this: God has spoken good concerning Israel; he will, in the end, make the triumph of the Philistines their own confusion; and the capture of the ark shall be the desolation of their gods; but the Israelites shall first be sorely pressed with calamity. Or, the affliction of the tabernacle, for all the wealth which God would have given Israel. <div eID="gen9553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9554" type="x-p"/> There shall not be an old man - This is repeated from the preceding verse, all the family shall die in the flower of their years, as is said in the following verse.
entries.5da60efc3f4d254c55bb5fc93ee2e257c7899bd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen9554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9555" type="x-p"/> And the man of thine - Of this passage Calmet observes: "The posterity of Eli possessed the high priesthood to the time of Solomon; and even when that dynasty was transferred to another family, God preserved that of Eli, not to render it more happy, but to punish it by seeing the prosperity of its enemies, to the end that it might see itself destitute and despised. This shows the depth of the judgments of God and the grandeur of his justice, which extends even to distant generations, and manifests itself to sinners both in life and death; both in their own disgrace, and in the prosperity of their enemies."
entries.2f494ff9c601dfe07d7d87aa5d2526f9725c8fd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen9555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9556" type="x-p"/> They shall die both of them - Hophni and Phinehas were both killed very shortly after in the great battle with the Philistines in which the Israelites were completely routed, and the ark taken. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1-1Sam.4.11">1Sam 4:1-11</reference>.
entries.2a5d81e6a106e5858fe71b5e1e7cce19dc45b458: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen9556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9557" type="x-p"/> A faithful priest - This seems to have been spoken of Zadok, who was anointed high priest in the room of Abiathar, the last descendant of the house of Eli; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.26">1Kgs 2:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.27">1Kgs 2:27</reference>. Abiathar was removed because he had joined with Adonijah, who had got himself proclaimed king; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.7">1Kgs 1:7</reference>. <div eID="gen9557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9558" type="x-p"/> I will build him a sure house - I will continue the priesthood in his family. <div eID="gen9558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9559" type="x-p"/> He shall walk before mine Anointed - He shall minister before Solomon, and the kings which shall reign in the land. The Targum says, "He shall walk קדם משיחי kodam Meshichi, before my Messiah," and the Septuagint expresses it, ενωπιον Χριστου μον, "before my Christ;" for, in their proper and more extended sense, these things are supposed to belong to our great High Priest and the Christian system: but the word may refer to the Israelitish people. See the note on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">Heb 9:26</reference>.
entries.b7b80ada77bb80f709295662e78a88fe53d08fdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen9559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9560" type="x-p"/> Shall come and crouch to him - Shall prostrate himself before him in the most abject manner, begging to be employed even in the meanest offices about the tabernacle, in order to get even the most scanty means of support. <div eID="gen9560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9561" type="x-p"/> A piece of silver - אגורת כסף agorath keseph, translated by the Septuagint, οβολου αργυριου, an obolus of silver. The Targum translates it מעא mea, which is the same as the Hebrew gerah, and weighed about sixteen grains of barley. <div eID="gen9561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9562" type="x-p"/> A morsel of bread - A mouthful; what might be sufficient to keep body and soul together. See the sin and its punishment. They formerly pampered themselves, and fed to the full on the Lord's sacrifices; and now they are reduced to a morsel of bread. They fed themselves without fear; and now they have cleanness of teeth in all their dwellings. They wasted the Lord's heritage, and now they beg their bread! <div eID="gen9562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9563" type="x-p"/> In religious establishments, vile persons, who have no higher motive, may and do get into the priest's office, that they may clothe themselves with the wool, and feed themselves with the fat, while they starve the flock. But where there is no law to back the claims of the worthless and the wicked, men of piety and solid merit only can find support; for they must live on the free-will offerings of the people. Where religion is established by law, the strictest ecclesiastical discipline should be kept up, and all hireling priests and ecclesiastical drones should be expelled from the Lord's vineyard. An established religion, where the foundation is good, as is ours, I consider a great blessing; but it is liable to this continual abuse, which nothing but careful and rigid ecclesiastical discipline can either cure or prevent. If our high priests, our archbishops and bishops, do not their duty, the whole body of the clergy may become corrupt or inefficient. If they be faithful, the establishment will be an honor to the kingdom, and a praise in the earth. <div eID="gen9563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9564" type="x-p"/> The words pillars of the earth, מצקי ארץ metsukey erets, Mr. Parkhurst translates and defends thus: "The compressors of the earth; i.e., the columns of the celestial fluid which compress or keep its parts together." This is all imaginary; we do not know this compressing celestial fluid; but there is one that answers the same end, which we do know, i.e., the Air, the columns of which press upon the earth in all directions; above, below, around, with a weight of fifteen pounds to every square inch; so that a column of air of the height of the atmosphere, which on the surface of the globe measures one square inch, is known by the most accurate and indubitable experiments to weigh fifteen pounds. Now as a square foot contains one hundred and forty-four square inches, each foot must be compressed with a weight of incumbent atmospheric air equal to two thousand one hundred and sixty pounds. And as the earth is known to contain a surface of five thousand five hundred and seventy-five billions of square feet; hence, allowing two thousand one hundred and sixty pounds to each square foot, the whole surface of the globe must sustain a pressure of atmospheric air equal to twelve trillions and forty-one thousand billions of pounds; or six thousand and twenty-one billions of tons. This pressure, independently of what is called gravity, is sufficient to keep all the parts of the earth together, and perhaps to counteract all the influence of centrifugal force. But adding to this all the influence of gravity or attraction, by which every particle of matter tends to the center, these compressors of the earth are sufficient to poise, balance, and preserve the whole terraqueous globe. These pillars or compressors are an astonishing provision made by the wisdom of God for the necessities of the globe. Without this, water could not rise in fountains, nor the sap in vegetables. Without this, there could be no respiration for man or beast, and no circulation of the blood in any animal. In short, both vegetable and animal life depend, under God, on these pillars or compressors of the earth; and were it not for this compressing power, the air contained in the vessels of all plants and animals would by its elasticity expand and instantly rupture all those vessels, and cause the destruction of all animal and vegetable life: but God in his wisdom has so balanced these two forces, that, while they appear to counteract and balance each other, they serve, by mutual dilations and compressions, to promote the circulation of the sap in vegetables, and the blood in animals.  <chapter eID="1Sam.2"/> <div eID="gen9564" type="x-p"/>

entries.50b22006f5810a0d7dabc90c3e039447db6c735e: <hi type="italic">Hannah’s song of praise</hi>. - The prayer in which Hannah poured out the feelings of her heart, after the dedication of her son to the Lord, is a song of praise of a prophetic and Messianic character. After giving utterance in the introduction to the rejoicing and exulting of her soul at the salvation that had reached her (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sa 2:1</reference>), she praises the Lord as the only holy One, the only rock of the righteous, who rules on earth with omniscience and righteousness, brings down the proud and lofty, kills and makes alive, maketh poor and maketh rich (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.2-1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:2-8</reference>). She then closes with the confident assurance that He will keep His saints, and cast down the rebellious, and will judge the ends of the earth, and exalt the power of His king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.9">1Sa 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.10">1Sa 2:10</reference>). <div eID="gen3644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3645" type="x-p"/> This psalm is the mature fruit of the Spirit of God. The pious woman, who had gone with all the earnest longings of a mother’s heart to pray to the Lord God of Israel for a son, that she might consecrate him to the lifelong service of the Lord, “discerned in her own individual experience the general laws of the divine economy, and its signification in relation to the whole history of the kingdom of God” (Auberlen, p. 564). The experience which she, bowed down and oppressed as she was, had had of the gracious government of the omniscient and holy covenant God, was a pledge to her of the gracious way in which the nation itself was led by God, and a sign by which she discerned how God not only delivered at all times the poor and wretched who trusted in Him out of their poverty and distress, and set them up, but would also lift up and glorify His whole nation, which was at that time so deeply bowed down and oppressed by its foes. Acquainted as she was with the destination of Israel to be a <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi>, from the promises which God had given to the patriarchs, and filled as she was with the longing that had been awakened in the nation for the realization of these promises, she could see in spirit, and through the inspiration of God, the <hi type="italic">king</hi> whom the Lord was about to give to His people, and through whom He would raise it up to might and dominion. <div eID="gen3645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3646" type="x-p"/> The refusal of modern critics to admit the genuineness of this song is founded upon an <hi type="italic">a priori</hi> and utter denial of the supernatural saving revelations of God, and upon a consequent inability to discern the prophetic illumination of the pious Hannah, and a complete misinterpretation of the contents of her song of praise. The “proud and lofty,” whom God humbles and casts down, are not the heathen or the national foes of Israel, and the “poor and wretched” whom He exalts and makes rich are not the Israelites as such; but the former are the <hi type="italic">ungodly</hi>, and the latter the <hi type="italic">pious</hi>, in Israel itself. And the description is so well sustained throughout, that it is only by the most arbitrary criticism that it can be interpreted as referring to definite historical events, such as the victory of David over Goliath (Thenius), or a victory of the Israelites over heathen nations (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and others). Still less can any argument be drawn from the words of the song in support of its later origin, or its composition by David or one of the earliest of the kings of Israel. On the contrary, not only is its genuineness supported by the general consideration that the author of these books would never have ascribed a song to Hannah, if he had not found it in the sources he employed; but still more decisively by the circumstance that the songs of praise of Mary and Zechariah, in Luk 1:46. and Luk 1:68., show, through the manner in which they rest upon this ode, in what way it was understood by the pious Israelites of every age, and how, like the pious Hannah, they recognised and praised in their own individual experience the government of the holy God in the midst of His kingdom. <div eID="gen3646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3647" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sa 2:1</reference> <div eID="gen3647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3648" type="x-p"/> The first verse forms the introduction to the song. Holy joy in the Lord at the blessing which she had received impelled the favoured mother to the praise of God: <div eID="gen3648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3649" type="x-p"/> 1  My heart is joyful in the Lord, <div eID="gen3649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3650" type="x-p"/> My horn is exalted in the Lord, <div eID="gen3650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3651" type="x-p"/> My mouth is opened wide over mine enemies: <div eID="gen3651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3652" type="x-p"/> For I rejoice in Thy salvation. <div eID="gen3652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3653" type="x-p"/> Of the four members of this verse, the first answers to the third, and the second to the fourth. The heart rejoices at the lifting up of her horn, the mouth opens wide to proclaim the salvation before which the enemies would be dumb. “<hi type="italic">My horn is high</hi>” does not mean 'I am proud' (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>), but “my power is great in the Lord.” The horn is the symbol of strength, and is taken from oxen whose strength is in their horns (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">Deu 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Psa 75:5</reference>, etc.). The power was high or exalted by the salvation which the Lord had manifested to her. To Him all the glory was due, because He had proved himself to be the holy One, and a rock upon which a man could rest his confidence.
entries.59f7650f358026e354ead3d32bb80ab5b70b7e0c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.2-1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen3653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3654" type="x-p"/> 2  None is holy as the Lord; for there is none beside Thee; <div eID="gen3654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3655" type="x-p"/> And no rock is as our God. <div eID="gen3655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3656" type="x-p"/> 3  Speak ye not much lofty, lofty; <div eID="gen3656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3657" type="x-p"/> Let (not) insolence go out of thy mouth! <div eID="gen3657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3658" type="x-p"/> For the Lord is an omniscient God, <div eID="gen3658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3659" type="x-p"/> And with Him deeds are weighed. <div eID="gen3659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3660" type="x-p"/> God manifests himself as holy in the government of the kingdom of His grace by His guidance of the righteous to salvation (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>). But holiness is simply the moral reflection of the glory of the one absolute God. This explains the reason given for His holiness, viz., “there is not one (a God) beside thee” (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.32">2Sa 22:32</reference>). As the holy and only One, God is the rock (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deu 32:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference>) in which the righteous can always trust. The wicked therefore should tremble before His holiness, and not talk in their pride of the <hi type="italic">lofty</hi> things which they have accomplished or intend to perform. גּבהה is defined more precisely in the following clause, which is also dependent upon אל by the word עתק, as insolent words spoken by the wicked against the righteous (see <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Psa 31:19</reference>). For Jehovah hears such words; He is “<hi type="italic">a God of knowledge</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Deus scientiarum</hi>), a God who sees and knows every single thing. The plural דּעות has an intensive signification. עללות נתכּנוּ לא might be rendered “deeds are not weighed, or equal” (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.25-Ezek.18.26">Eze 18:25-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.17">Eze 33:17</reference>). But this would only apply to the actions of men; for the acts of God are always just, or weighed. But an assertion respecting the actions of men does not suit the context. Hence this clause is reckoned in the Masora as one of the passages in which לא stands for לו (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.21.8">Exo 21:8</reference>). “<hi type="italic">To Him</hi> (with Him) <hi type="italic">deeds are weighed</hi>:” that is to say, the acts of God are weighed, i.e., equal or just. This is the real meaning according to the passages in Ezekiel, and not “the actions of men are weighed by Him” (De Wette, Maurer, <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, etc.): for God weighs the minds and hearts of men (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">Pro 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.12">Pro 24:12</reference>), not their actions. This expression never occurs. The weighed or righteous acts of God are described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4-1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:4-8</reference> in great and general traits, as displayed in the government of His kingdom through the marvellous changes which occur in the circumstances connected with the lives of the righteous and the wicked.
entries.4e89c322532ecf925cc1d0c408e1a4639a5e39ec: 1Sa 2:4-8   4  Bow-heroes are confounded, <div eID="gen3660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3661" type="x-p"/> And stumbling ones gird themselves with strength;   5  Full ones hire themselves out for bread, <div eID="gen3661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3662" type="x-p"/> And hungry ones cease to be. <div eID="gen3662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3663" type="x-p"/> Yea, the barren beareth seven (children), <div eID="gen3663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3664" type="x-p"/> And she that is rich in children pines away.   6  The Lord kills and makes alive; <div eID="gen3664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3665" type="x-p"/> Leads down into hell, and leads up.   7  The Lord makes poor and makes rich, <div eID="gen3665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3666" type="x-p"/> Humbles and also exalts.   8  He raises mean ones out of the dust, <div eID="gen3666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3667" type="x-p"/> He lifts up poor ones out of the dunghill, <div eID="gen3667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3668" type="x-p"/> To set them beside the noble; <div eID="gen3668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3669" type="x-p"/> And He apportions to them the seat of glory: <div eID="gen3669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3670" type="x-p"/> For the pillars of the earth are the Lord's, <div eID="gen3670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3671" type="x-p"/> And He sets the earth upon them. <div eID="gen3671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3672" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4">1Sa 2:4</reference>, the predicate חתּים is construed with the <hi type="italic">nomen rectum</hi> גּבּרים, not with the <hi type="italic">nomen regens</hi> קשׁת, because the former is the leading term (vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §148, 1, and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §317, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.). The thought to be expressed is, not that the bow itself is to be broken, but that the heroes who carry the bow are to be confounded or broken inwardly. “<hi type="italic">Bows of the heroes</hi>” stands for heroes carrying bows. For this reason the verb is to be taken in the sense of confounded, not broken, especially as, apart from <reference osisRef="Jer.51.56">Jer 51:56</reference>, חתת is not used to denote the breaking of outward things, but the breaking of men.
entries.7e8f57f5de012159df37d87642202abd1d2f3713: 1Sa 2:9-10   9  The feet of His saints He will keep, <div eID="gen3672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3673" type="x-p"/> And the wicked perish in darkness; <div eID="gen3673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3674" type="x-p"/> For by power no one becomes strong. 10  The Lord - those who contend against Him are confounded. <div eID="gen3674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3675" type="x-p"/> He thunders above him in the heavens; <div eID="gen3675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3676" type="x-p"/> The Lord will judge the ends of the earth, <div eID="gen3676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3677" type="x-p"/> That He may lend might to His king, And exalt the horn of His anointed. <div eID="gen3677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3678" type="x-p"/> The Lord keeps the feet of the righteous, so that they do not tremble and stumble, i.e., so that the righteous do not fall into adversity and perish therein (vid., Ps. 56:14; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.8">Psa 116:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference>). But the wicked, who oppress and persecute the righteous, will perish in darkness, i.e., in adversity, when God withdraws the light of His grace, so that they fall into distress and calamity. For no man can be strong through his own power, so as to meet the storms of life. All who fight against the Lord are destroyed. To bring out the antithesis between man and God, “Jehovah” is written absolutely at the commencement of the sentence in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.10">1Sa 2:10</reference> : “<hi type="italic">As for Jehovah, those who contend against Him are broken</hi>,” both inwardly and outwardly (חתת, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4">1Sa 2:4</reference>). The word עלו, which follows, is not to be changed into עליהם. There is simply a rapid alternation of the numbers, such as we frequently meet with in excited language. “<hi type="italic">Above him</hi>,” i.e., above every one who contends against God, He thunders. Thunder is a premonitory sign of the approach of the Lord to judgment. In the thunder, man is made to feel in an alarming way the presence of the omnipotent God. In the words, “<hi type="italic">The Lord will judge the ends of the earth</hi>,” i.e., the earth to its utmost extremities, or the whole world, Hannah’s prayer rises up to a prophetic glance at the consummation of the kingdom of God. As certainly as the Lord God keeps the righteous at all times, and casts down the wicked, so certainly will He judge the whole world, to hurl down all His foes, and perfect His kingdom which He has founded in Israel. And as every kingdom culminates in its throne, or in the full might and government of a king, so the kingdom of God can only attain its full perfection in the king whom the Lord will give to His people, and endow with His might. <hi type="italic">The king</hi>, or the <hi type="italic">anointed of the Lord</hi>, of whom Hannah prophesies in the spirit, is not one single king of Israel, either David or Christ, but an ideal king, though not a mere personification of the throne about to be established, but the actual king whom Israel received in David and his race, which culminated in the Messiah. The exaltation of the horn of the anointed to Jehovah commenced with the victorious and splendid expansion of the power of David, was repeated with every victory over the enemies of God and His kingdom gained by the successive kings of David’s house, goes on in the advancing spread of the kingdom of Christ, and will eventually attain to its eternal consummation in the judgment of the last day, through which all the enemies of Christ will be made His footstool.<hi type="italic">Samuel the servant of the Lord under Eli. Ungodliness of the sons of Eli</hi>. -  <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.11">1Sa 2:11</reference> forms the transition to what follows. After Hannah’s psalm of thanksgiving, Elkanah went back with his family to his home at Ramah, and the boy (Samuel) was serving, i.e., ministered to the Lord, in the presence of Eli the priest. The fact that nothing is said about Elkanah’s wives going with him, does not warrant the interpretation given by Thenius, that Elkanah went home alone. It was taken for granted that his wives went with him, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.21">1Sa 1:21</reference> (“all his house”). את־יחוה שׁרת, which signifies literally, both here and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1Sa 3:1</reference>, to serve the Lord, and which is used interchangeably with יי את־פּני שׁרת (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.18">1Sa 2:18</reference>), to serve in the presence of the Lord, is used to denote the duties performed both by priests and Levites in connection with the worship of God, in which Samuel took part, as he grew up, under the superintendence of Eli and according to his instruction.
entries.3793b693b2d76042d0aa3e68e98d1bf11bda62fa: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.12">1Sa 2:12</reference> <div eID="gen3678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3679" type="x-p"/> But Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.34">1Sa 2:34</reference>), were בליּעל בּני, worthless fellows, and knew not the Lord, sc., as He should be known, i.e., did not fear Him, or trouble themselves about Him (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference>; Hos 8:2; Hos 13:4).
entries.6840f4d5fd020cb0e66d2f69da46fecdf67dff9a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13-1Sam.2.14">1Sa 2:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen3679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3680" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And the right of the priests towards the people was</hi> (the following).” <hi type="italic">Mishpat</hi> signifies the right which they had usurped to themselves in relation to the people. “<hi type="italic">If any one brought a sacrifice</hi> (זבח זבח כּל־אישׁ is placed first, and construed absolutely: 'as for every one who brought a slain-offering'), <hi type="italic">the priest’s servant</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. young man) <hi type="italic">came while the flesh was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand, and thrust into the kettle, or pot, or bowl, or saucepan. All that the fork brought up the priest took. This they did to all the Israelites who came thither to Shiloh</hi>.”
entries.04ab17e3e07d8fb245ff83926b4c2554ba53e19c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.15-1Sam.2.16">1Sa 2:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen3680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3681" type="x-p"/> They did still worse. “<hi type="italic">Even before the fat was consumed</hi>,” i.e., before the fat portions of the sacrifice had been placed in the altar-fire for the Lord (<reference osisRef="Lev.3.3-Lev.3.5">Lev 3:3-5</reference>), the priest’s servant came and demanded flesh of the person sacrificing, to be roasted for the priest; “<hi type="italic">for he will not take boiled flesh of thee, but only</hi> חי, <hi type="italic">raw</hi>, i.e., fresh meat.” And if the person sacrificing replied, “<hi type="italic">They will burn the fat directly</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. 'at this time,' as in <reference osisRef="Gen.25.31">Gen 25:31</reference>; 1Ki 22:5), <hi type="italic">then take for thyself, as thy soul desireth</hi>,” he said, “<hi type="italic">No</hi> (לו for לא), <hi type="italic">but thou shalt give now; if not, I take by force</hi>.” These abuses were practised by the priests in connection with the thank-offerings, with which a sacrificial meal was associated. Of these offerings, with which a sacrificial meal was associated. Of these offerings, the portion which legally fell to the priest as his share was the heave-leg and wave-breast. And this he was to receive after the fat portions of the sacrifice had been burned upon the altar (see <reference osisRef="Lev.7.30-Lev.7.34">Lev 7:30-34</reference>). To take the flesh of the sacrificial animal and roast it before this offering had been made, was a crime which was equivalent to a robbery of God, and is therefore referred to here with the emphatic particle גּם, as being the worst crime that the sons of Eli committed. Moreover, the priests could not claim any of the flesh which the offerer of the sacrifice boiled for the sacrificial meal, after burning the fat portions upon the altar and giving up the portions which belonged to them, to say nothing of their taking it forcibly out of the pots while it was being boiled.
entries.6d22a39c09406f17c072af8403ecb0a48f6d91bf: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.17">1Sa 2:17</reference> <div eID="gen3681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3682" type="x-p"/> Such conduct as this on the part of the young men (the priests’ servants), was a great sin in the sight of the Lord, as they thereby brought the sacrifice of the Lord into contempt. נאץ, causative, to bring into contempt, furnish occasion for blaspheming (as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.14">2Sa 12:14</reference>). “The robbery which they committed was a small sin in comparison with the contempt of the sacrifices themselves, which they were the means of spreading among the people” (<hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>). <hi type="italic">Minchah</hi> does not refer here to the meat-offering as the accompaniment to the slain-offerings, but to the sacrificial offering generally, as a gift presented for the Lord.<hi type="italic">Samuel’s service before the Lord</hi>. - 1Sa 2:18. Samuel served as a boy before the Lord by the side of the worthless sons of Eli, girt with an ephod of white material (בּד, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.28.42">Exo 28:42</reference>). The ephod was a shoulder-dress, no doubt resembling the high priest’s in shape (see Exo 28:6.), but altogether different in the material of which it was made, viz., simple white cloth, like the other articles of clothing that were worn by the priests. At that time, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.18">1Sa 22:18</reference>, all the priests wore clothing of this kind; and, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.14">2Sa 6:14</reference>, David did the same on the occasion of a religious festival. Samuel received a dress of this kind even when a boy, because he was set apart to a lifelong service before the Lord. חגוּר is the technical expression for putting on the ephod, because the two pieces of which it was composed were girt round the body with a girdle.
entries.ade3547f10d292ef6f6bbc50d3463da15498ea03: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.19">1Sa 2:19</reference> <div eID="gen3682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3683" type="x-p"/> The small מעיל also (<hi type="italic">Angl</hi>. “coat”), which Samuel’s mother made and brought him every year, when she came with her husband to Shiloh to the yearly sacrifice, was probably a coat resembling the <hi type="italic">meïl</hi> of the high priest (Exo 28:31.), but was made of course of some simpler material, and without the symbolical ornaments attached to the lower hem, by which that official dress was distinguished.
entries.a2df54f55189535529ed627d0c71cbda96303cda: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.20">1Sa 2:20</reference> <div eID="gen3683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3684" type="x-p"/> The priestly clothing of the youthful Samuel was in harmony with the spiritual relation in which he stood to the high priest and to Jehovah. Eli blessed his parents for having given up the boy to the Lord, and expressed this wish to the father: “<hi type="italic">The Lord lend thee seed of this woman in the place of the one asked for</hi> (השּׁאלה), <hi type="italic">whom they</hi> (one) <hi type="italic">asked for from the Lord</hi>.” The striking use of the third pers. masc. שׁאל instead of the second singular or plural may be accounted for on the supposition that it is an indefinite form of speech, which the writer chose because, although it was Hannah who prayed to the Lord for Samuel in the sight of Eli, yet Eli might assume that the father, Elkanah, had shared the wishes of his pious wife. The apparent harshness disappears at once if we substitute the passive; whereas in Hebrew active constructions were always preferred to passive, wherever it was possible to employ them (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §294, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). The singular suffix attached to למקומו after the plural הלכוּ may be explained on the simple ground, that a dwelling-place is determined by the husband, or master of the house.
entries.c8c4d75c04984ef84888e062b404bca8b92b3b7d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.21">1Sa 2:21</reference> <div eID="gen3684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3685" type="x-p"/> The particle כּי, “<hi type="italic">for</hi>” (Jehovah visited), does not mean <hi type="italic">if</hi>, <hi type="italic">as</hi>, or <hi type="italic">when</hi>, nor is it to be regarded as a copyist’s error. It is only necessary to supply the thought contained in the words, “<hi type="italic">Eli blessed Elkanah</hi>,” viz., that Eli’s blessing was not an empty fruitless wish; and to understand the passage in some such way as this: Eli’s word was fulfilled, or still more simply, <hi type="italic">they went to their home blessed</hi>; for <hi type="italic">Jehovah visited Hannah</hi>, blessed her with “<hi type="italic">three sons and two daughters; but the boy Samuel grew up with the Lord</hi>,” i.e., near to Him (at the sanctuary), and under His protection and blessing.<hi type="italic">Eli’s treatment of the sins of his sons</hi>. - 1Sa 2:22. The aged Eli reproved his sons with solemn warnings on account of their sins; but without his warnings being listened to. From the reproof itself we learn, that beside the sin noticed in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.12-1Sam.2.17">1Sa 2:12-17</reference>, they also committed the crime of lying with the women who served at the tabernacle (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.38.8">Exo 38:8</reference>), and thus profaned the sanctuary with whoredom. But Eli, with the infirmities of his old age, did nothing further to prevent these abominations than to say to his sons, “<hi type="italic">Why do ye according to the sayings which I hear, sayings about you which are evil, of this whole people</hi>.” רעים את־דּבריכם is inserted to make the meaning clearer, and כּל־ה מאת is dependent upon שׁמע. “<hi type="italic">This whole people</hi>” signifies all the people that came to Shiloh, and heard and saw the wicked doings there.
entries.b25fa7ece1fb9054f49266f8f1cdc0f727130106: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.24">1Sa 2:24</reference> בּני אל, “<hi type="italic">Not, my sons</hi>,” i.e., do not such things, “<hi type="italic">for the report which I hear is not good; they make the people of Jehovah to transgress</hi>.” מערים is written without the pronoun אתּם in an indefinite construction, like משׁלּחים in <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.3">1Sa 6:3</reference> (Maurer). <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>'s rendering as given by Thenius, “The report which I hear the people of God bring,” is just as inadmissible as the one proposed by Böttcher, “The report which, as I hear, the people of God are spreading.” The assertion made by Thenius, that העביר, without any further definition, cannot mean to cause to sin or transgress, is correct enough no doubt; but it does not prove that this meaning is inadmissible in the passage before us, since the further definition is actually to be found in the context.
entries.62b2d1b34dfd7290be92b3f73162da8b77e06e99: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.25">1Sa 2:25</reference> <div eID="gen3685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3686" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">If man sins against man, God judges him; but if a man sins against Jehovah, who can interpose with entreaty for him</hi>?” In the use of פּללו and יתפּלּל־לו there is a paranomasia which cannot be reproduced in our language. פּלּל signifies to decide or pass sentence (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.11">Gen 48:11</reference>), then to arbitrate, to settle a dispute as arbitrator (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.52">Eze 16:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.30">Psa 106:30</reference>), and in the <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi> to act as mediator, hence to entreat. And these meanings are applicable here. In the case of one man’s sin against another, God settles the dispute as arbitrator through the proper authorities; whereas, when a man sins against God, no one can interpose as arbitrator. Such a sin cannot be disposed of by intercession. But Eli’s sons did not listen to this admonition, which was designed to reform daring sinners with mild words and representation; “<hi type="italic">for</hi>,” adds the historian, “<hi type="italic">Jehovah was resolved to slay them</hi>.” The father’s reproof made no impression upon them, because they were already given up to the judgment of hardening. (On hardening as a divine sentence, see the discussions at Exo 4:21.)
entries.9350a801f59f690879eda5290a136c3bcc9adf01: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.26">1Sa 2:26</reference> <div eID="gen3686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3687" type="x-p"/> The youthful Samuel, on the other hand, continued to grow in stature, and in favour with God and man (see <reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Luk 2:52</reference>).
entries.10b2c033961c57608777926f57afa2e859a8935c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27-1Sam.2.36">1Sa 2:27-36</reference> <hi type="italic">Announcement of the judgment upon Eli and his house</hi>. - 1Sa 2:27. Before the Lord interposed in judgment, He sent a prophet (a “<hi type="italic">man of God</hi>,” as in Jdg 13:6) to the aged Eli, to announce as a warning for all ages the judgment which was about to fall upon the worthless priests of his house. In order to arouse Eli’s own conscience, he had pointed out to him, on the one hand, the grace manifested in the choice of his father’s house, i.e., the house of Aaron, to keep His sanctuary (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27">1Sa 2:27</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.28">1Sa 2:28</reference>), and, on the other hand, the desecration of the sanctuary by the wickedness of his sons (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.29">1Sa 2:29</reference>). Then follows the sentence: The choice of the family of Aaron still stood fast, but the deepest disgrace would come upon the despisers of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1Sa 2:30</reference>): the strength of his house would be broken; all the members of his house were to die early deaths. They were not, however, to be removed entirely from service at the altar, but to their sorrow were to survive the fall of the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.31-1Sam.2.34">1Sa 2:31-34</reference>). But the Lord would raise up a faithful priest, and cause him to walk before His anointed, and from him all that were left of the house of Eli would be obliged to beg their bread (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.35">1Sa 2:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.36">1Sa 2:36</reference>). To arrive at the true interpretation of this announcement of punishment, we must picture to ourselves the historical circumstances that come into consideration here. Eli the high priest was a descendant of Ithamar, the younger son of Aaron, as we may see from the fact that his great-grandson Ahimelech was “of the sons of Ithamar” (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference>). In perfect agreement with this, Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. v. 11, 5) relates, that after the high priest Ozi of the family of Eleazar, Eli of the family of Ithamar received the high-priesthood. The circumstances which led to the transfer of this honour from the line of Eleazar to that of Ithamar are unknown. We cannot imagine it to have been occasioned by an extinction of the line of Eleazar, for the simple reason that, in the time of David, Zadok the descendant of Eleazar is spoken of as high priest along with Abiathar and Ahimelech, the descendants of Eli (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2Sa 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2Sa 20:25</reference>). After the deposition of Abiathar he was reinstated by Solomon as sole high priest (1Ki 2:27), and the dignity was transmitted to his descendants. This fact also overthrows the conjecture of Clericus, that the transfer of the high-priesthood to Eli took place by the command of God on account of the grievous sins of the high priests of the line of Eleazar; for in that case Zadok would not have received this office again in connection with Abiathar. We have, no doubt, to search for the true reason in the circumstances of the times of the later judges, namely in the fact that at the death of the last high priest of the family of Eleazar before the time of Eli, the remaining son was not equal to the occasion, either because he was still an infant, or at any rate because he was too young and inexperienced, so that he could not enter upon the office, and Eli, who was probably related by marriage to the high priest’s family, and was no doubt a vigorous man, was compelled to take the oversight of the congregation; and, together with the supreme administration of the affairs of the nation as judge, received the post of high priest as well, and filled it till the time of his death, simply because in those troublous times there was not one of the descendants of Eleazar who was able to fill the supreme office of judge, which was combined with that of high priest. For we cannot possibly think of an unjust usurpation of the office of high priest on the part of Eli, since the very judgment denounced against him and his house presupposes that he had entered upon the office in a just and upright way, and that the wickedness of his sons was all that was brought against him. For a considerable time after the death of Eli the high-priesthood lost almost all its significance. All Israel turned to Samuel, whom the Lord established as His prophet by means of revelations, and whom He also chose as the deliverer of His people. The tabernacle at Shiloh, which ceased to be the scene of the gracious presence of God after the loss of the ark, was probably presided over first of all after Eli’s death by his grandson Ahitub, the son of Phinehas, as his successor in the high-priesthood. He was followed in the time of Saul by his son Ahijah or Ahimelech, who gave David the shew-bread to eat at Nob, to which the tabernacle had been removed in the meantime, and was put to death by Saul in consequence, along with all the priests who were found there. His son Abiathar, however, escaped the massacre, and fled to David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.20">1Sa 22:9-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:6</reference>). In the reign of David he is mentioned as high priest along with Zadok; but he was afterwards deposed by Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.24">2Sa 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.15">2Sa 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.12">2Sa 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2Sa 20:25</reference>; 1Ki 2:27). <div eID="gen3687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3688" type="x-p"/> Different interpretations have been given of these verses. The majority of commentators understand them as signifying that the loss of the high-priesthood is here foretold to Eli, and also the institution of Zadok in the office. But such a view is too contracted, and does not exhaust the meaning of the words. The very introduction to the prophet’s words points to something greater than this: “<hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord, Did I reveal myself to thy father’s house, when they were in Egypt at the house of Pharaoh</hi>?” The ה interrogative is not used for הלא (<hi type="italic">nonne</hi>), but is emphatic, as in Jer 31:20. The question is an appeal to Eli’s conscience, which he cannot deny, but is obliged to confirm. By Eli’s father’s house we are not to understand Ithamar and his family, but Aaron, from whom Eli was descended through Ithamar. God revealed himself to the tribe-father of Eli by appointing Aaron to be the spokesman of Moses before Pharaoh (Exo 4:14. and <reference osisRef="Exod.4.27">Exo 4:27</reference>), and still more by calling Aaron to the priesthood, for which the way was prepared by the fact that, from the very beginning, God made use of Aaron, in company with Moses, to carry out His purpose of delivering Israel out of Egypt, and entrusted Moses and Aaron with the arrangements for the celebration of the passover (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.1">Exo 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.43">Exo 12:43</reference>). This occurred when they, the fathers of Eli, Aaron and his sons, were still in Egypt at the house of Pharaoh, i.e., still under Pharaoh’s rule.
entries.47a48f0002acac293168220b1a0c5c91c82f1965: <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.28">1Sa 2:28</reference> <div eID="gen3688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3689" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And did I choose him out of all the tribes for a priest to myself</hi>.” The interrogative particle is not to be repeated before וּבחור, but the construction becomes affirmative with the inf. abs. instead of the perfect. “<hi type="italic">Him</hi>” refers back to “<hi type="italic">thy father</hi>” in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27">1Sa 2:27</reference>, and signifies Aaron.
